summary: ECHO (Earth-Comparable Habitats Observatory) is a planetary analog research workspace that aims to make exploring comparative environments between Earth's environments and those found on other planets simpler. Specifically, ECHO allows users to navigate through a combination of NASA planetary data reference sources as well as Earth analog regions all within one interface. The goal is to provide source records/evidence in close proximity when making these kinds of comparisons. The primary user challenges addressed by ECHO include both the ability to more easily perform this kind of research as well as effectively convey the findings. Through ECHO, users can pick their target planet and objectives, then see candidate regions for consideration. They then get terrain datasets to evaluate as well as measurements about the elevations, slopes and roughness of samples taken at specific sites.(Note This current version of the tool makes use of NASA data and services [e.g., Earthdata, PDS] but separates out the measured results of samples vs illustrative content). As such, this tool can aid them in developing plans for conducting future observation studies. However, please note that this is just a research prototype and the candidate regions have not been proven to be true analogs nor have the current selections for terrain samples been determined to scientifically meet any criteria for suitability.
details:
Project Details:

ECHO (Earth-Comparable Habitats Observatory) is a research prototype that helps users explore Earth terrain in the context of Moon and Mars missions. It combines mission planning, candidate-region exploration, NASA data references, and sample terrain comparisons in one workspace. Using local NASADEM and LRO LOLA samples, it calculates elevation range, slope, and roughness. Candidate sites are leads for investigation—not confirmed analogs—and the measurements do not establish mission suitability.

What does it do or how does our project work:

ECHO helps users explore Earth regions as possible analogs for Moon and Mars mission research. Users select a target body and objective, browse candidate regions, and review NASA data references and terrain evidence. For local Atacama and lunar South Pole samples, it calculates elevation range, slope, and roughness. Results are exploratory and do not confirm analog suitability.

Benefits of ECH

ECHO brings mission planning, Earth analog research leads, and NASA data references into one workspace, reducing the need to search across separate catalogs and tools. It keeps source links, resolution, processing notes, and data gaps close to each comparison, making evidence easier to inspect and discuss. Users can review descriptive terrain measures—elevation range, slope, and roughness—for local Atacama and lunar South Pole samples, helping them identify questions and locations for further investigation. These exploratory comparisons support research planning; they do not confirm analog suitability or replace expert review.

The intended impact of our project:

ECHO aims to make early planetary analog research more transparent and easier to explore. By bringing candidate Earth regions, NASA data references, terrain measurements, and provenance into one workspace, it can help researchers and mission planners identify areas that merit closer study, compare available evidence, and see where important data is missing. This may support better-informed planning for future observations, fieldwork, and instrument studies.

The intended impact is to improve how teams organize and communicate early-stage comparisons—not to certify landing sites or determine mission suitability. ECHO is a prototype, and its candidate regions and sample measurements require further scientific validation before they can support operational decisions.

Tools, coding languages, hardware, or software we used to develop our project :

ECHO was developed on a standard Windows computer; no specialized scientific hardware was required. The frontend uses React 19 and TypeScript, built with Vite, with Tailwind CSS for styling, Leaflet and React-Leaflet for maps, and Recharts for data visualizations. The backend uses Python 3.13, FastAPI, and Uvicorn, with Pydantic for data validation and Rasterio and NumPy for processing terrain samples.

The application connects to NASA Earthdata CMR metadata and NASA PDS product records, and supports USGS geology point queries. Render hosts the frontend and API, while GitHub is used for source control and deployment. Visual Studio Code was used for development. AI assistance was used for coding and debugging support; the team reviewed the implementation, and AI was not used to generate scientific findings or validate analog suitability.

Our project's creativity :

Our ECHO’s creativity lies in bringing planetary mission planning, Earth analog research leads, NASA data references, and terrain evidence into one inspectable workspace. Instead of presenting a similarity score as a conclusion, it separates measured sample terrain from illustrative content and keeps sources, processing details, and data gaps visible. This gives researchers a clearer starting point for asking which environments merit further investigation, while leaving scientific judgment and validation to people.

What factors we considered :

We considered the mission objective and target body, the terrain characteristics relevant to exploration, and the quality and limits of available evidence. For the prototype comparison, we used local NASADEM data for an Atacama sample and NASA LRO LOLA data for a lunar South Pole sample. We examined elevation range, slope, and local roughness, while recording each sample’s source, coverage, resolution, projection, and processing. The Earth and lunar datasets come from different instruments and vertical references, so their measurements are exploratory and do not establish environmental equivalence or mission suitability.

We also considered data gaps, spatial coverage, resolution differences, and the need to distinguish measured sample results from illustrative map content and scores. Candidate regions are research leads that need further validation.

For Lonar Crater background, our project references V. K. Nayak’s 1992 NASA NTRS conference paper, A History of the Lonar Crater, India: An Overview. It informs the crater’s geological context; it is not a validation study for ECHO’s comparison method. NASA NTRS record
